reception.text: In Joseph Bucklin Bishop's telling, J. P. Morgan came to the White House proposing that his lawyer and the Attorney General "fix it up"; Roosevelt said it could not be done.
reception.source: Joseph Bucklin Bishop, Theodore Roosevelt and His Time (1920), I:184–85

reception.text: The 1904 Democratic platform attacked the administration's "headstrong, arbitrary and spasmodic methods" while also demanding stricter enforcement against the trusts.
Justice Holmes's Northern Securities dissent, with its line "Great cases like hard cases make bad law," became nearly as famous as the ruling, and Roosevelt called Holmes "a bitter disappointment."
reception.source: 193 U.S. 400; Roosevelt to Lodge, TRC libID o196434

political_impact.text: Roosevelt leaked to the Associated Press, without attribution, that six senators had received telegrams signed "John D. Rockefeller" opposing antitrust legislation; the bill strengthening the Bureau of Corporations then passed.
political_impact.source: Morning Press (Santa Barbara), February 8, 1903; Edmund Morris, Theodore Rex, p. 642 n.

political_impact.text: Congress created the Department of Commerce and Labor with a Bureau of Corporations empowered to investigate interstate corporations and publish what the President chose to release.

James R. Garfield became the first Commissioner of Corporations, and the Bureau published reports on beef, petroleum transportation, the petroleum industry, cotton exchanges and tobacco during Roosevelt's presidency.

The Bureau's 1906 report on petroleum transportation, documenting secret rates and rebates for Standard Oil, fed directly into Roosevelt's special message asking Congress to enlarge the Interstate Commerce Commission's powers.
The Supreme Court affirmed the dissolution of the Northern Securities Company five to four, with no majority opinion.
political_impact.source: Northern Securities Co. v. United States, 193 U.S. 197

political_impact.text: E. H. Harriman, bought out of the company in 1901, sued to get his railroad shares back after the breakup.
political_impact.source: Harriman v. Northern Securities Co., 197 U.S. 244

legacy.text: The Federal Trade Commission Act provided that the Bureau of Corporations would cease to exist once the Commission organized, with its staff, records and pending investigations passing to the FTC.
The Federal Trade Commission organized on March 16, 1915, the day the Bureau actually ended.
The largest antitrust breakups came after Roosevelt left office, in the Standard Oil and American Tobacco decisions of May 1911.
By the Justice Department's count, Roosevelt's administration started 44 antitrust proceedings in seven and a half years and Taft's started 90 in four.
legacy.source: Eliot Jones, The Trust Problem in the United States (1921), p. 444

legacy.text: The Bureau's steel-industry report, Part I, came out under Taft in 1911; the Bureau published nothing on steel during Roosevelt's presidency.
legacy.source: Report of the Commissioner of Corporations on the Steel Industry, Part I (1911)

today.name: Federal Trade Commission
today.note: The Bureau of Corporations' staff, records and investigations passed to the FTC in 1915.
